name: Ductless Mini‑Split vs Central Air for Small Los Angeles Bungalows

mainEntity.name: How do I compare ductless mini‑split vs central air for a small Los Angeles bungalow with limited attic space?
mainEntity.text: How do I compare ductless mini‑split vs central air for a small Los Angeles bungalow with limited attic space?

acceptedAnswer.text: Comparing ductless mini‑splits and central air for a small Los Angeles bungalow comes down to your attic space, layout, and comfort preferences. If you have almost no usable attic or crawl space, running new ducts can be invasive, require soffits, and trigger extra drywall and finish work. In these homes, ductless mini‑splits often shine because they require only small wall penetrations for refrigerant lines and no bulky duct runs. Ductless systems also provide zone control, allowing you to cool bedrooms and living areas independently, which can lower energy use when parts of the house sit empty. They generally deliver high efficiency ratings and can be easier to install in older homes with plaster walls or limited structural cavities. Central air is more appealing if you already have quality ducts or are planning a remodel that opens ceilings and walls anyway. Central systems keep equipment mostly hidden, use one main thermostat, and can be paired with existing forced-air heating. When comparing quotes, look at total installed cost (including drywall repair), equipment efficiency, indoor aesthetics, and noise levels. Ask each contractor to explain how they would run ducts or mini‑split lines in your specific bungalow, then weigh the disruption versus comfort benefits.
acceptedAnswer.description: For a small Los Angeles bungalow with little attic space, ductless mini‑splits avoid new ductwork, offer zone control, and often cost less to install than reworking tight ducts. Central air may be better if you already have good ducts or want whole‑home cooling with a single thermostat and hidden equipment.
